title: How to Fact-Check AI Output Before You Publish (2026 Guide)

A four-step fact-checking routine for AI-assisted drafts: extract the claims, classify by risk, verify each type, run a red-flag sweep.

AI-assisted drafts fail fact-checking in a specific way. They rarely produce obvious nonsense; they produce text that is mostly right, with the remaining errors wearing the same confident tone as everything around them. That is what makes publishing AI output risky — the mistakes are not marked as mistakes, and a reader has no way to tell which line you checked.

The answer is not to stop using drafts. It is to run a verification pass with a fixed shape, so checking takes a focused half hour instead of becoming an open-ended suspicion. This guide sets out four steps and a checklist you can apply to anything before it goes out.

What models actually get wrong

Five categories cover most of what slips through:

  • Invented figures — statistics with decimal places, sample sizes and dates that were never published anywhere.
  • Source drift — a real study described accurately but used to support a narrower claim than it actually makes.
  • Fabricated references — correct-looking citations with the wrong year, volume or pairing of authors.
  • Stale facts — statements that were true of an earlier rule, an older product version or a previous model release.
  • Lost hedging — "may be associated with" becomes "causes", because the hedge was the least memorable part of the sentence.

None of this requires malice. It is an artefact of a system that produces the most probable continuation of your prompt, and probability is not the same thing as provenance.

Frequency matters as much as type. Errors cluster at the joints — the specific number inside a generally true sentence, the date attached to a real event, the name of the person who said the quote. Anything sitting at a joint earns the full check; the surrounding prose can usually take a lighter one.

Step 1: Extract every checkable claim

Open the draft and list every statement a reader could verify: numbers, dates, names, cause-and-effect claims, quotations, legal and regulatory claims, and any sentence containing "studies show" or "according to". Do this before you argue with the content, because familiarity makes claims feel already verified.

You can ask the model to help: list every factual claim in this draft, with the sentence it appears in. Then read the list yourself, because a model will occasionally classify its own invention as an opinion, which keeps it off the checklist in the most convenient way possible.

Expect more claims than you thought. A short draft usually carries a dozen checkable statements, and most writers have only ever verified three of them — usually the ones they were already unsure about.

Step 2: Classify by risk

Not every claim deserves the same effort. Sort the list into three tiers and spend your time where an error would be expensive.

TierExamplesStandard of check
HighNumbers, quotes, laws, names of people and organisationsPrimary source, opened yourself
MediumTrends, comparisons, causal claimsTwo independent sources
LowFraming, background, opinionRead for plausibility, label as judgement

High-tier claims are the ones that end in corrections pages. A wrong number gets quoted onward, a misattributed quote reaches the person you attributed it to, and a legal statement gets repeated by readers who never saw your hedge. Everything lower can survive a lighter check, provided the piece does not rest on it.

Step 3: Verify each type the right way

Verification means opening the source, not asking another model. For figures, find the original report or dataset and confirm the number, the population it describes and the year it covers. For quotations, find the exact words in the original and confirm speaker, context and wording. For legal and regulatory claims, go to the official text rather than a summary of it. If you are quoting at length rather than briefly, our AI copyright guide covers what generally needs permission.

For claims you cannot source directly, apply a rule of two: two independent sources that do not cite each other. Independence matters more than quantity — five articles repeating one wire story are one source wearing five coats.

What it means for you: the check should leave a trail. Keep the link or document beside each verified claim, so a colleague, an editor or a future you can confirm it without repeating the search. Unverified but flagged is a legitimate state; undocumented verification is not verification.

Step 4: The red-flag sweep

Before publishing, read the draft once looking only for warning signs. Precise figures with no source attached. Universal claims such as always, never and everyone. Causal language built on correlational evidence. Recent regulatory, medical or financial statements, which change faster than any model's training data. Sentences more confident than a careful expert would say out loud.

Then check the quotations and the first and last paragraphs, where framing errors do the most damage and where AI drafts are most likely to open with a claim they never support.

Read once more for what is missing rather than what is wrong. AI drafts leave out counter-arguments, exceptions and the caveat that qualifies a broad claim, because an omission never looks like an error while you are reading. If a section would surprise the person who knows the topic best, find out why before you publish it.

What it means for you: this pass costs a few minutes and catches the class of error readers notice first — a confident claim that turns out to be wrong, sitting inside a piece otherwise full of correct ones. Trust is lost on the visible mistake, not on the invisible ones.

The pre-publish checklist

Run this before anything leaves your hands:

  1. Every checkable claim is listed, not only the ones you already doubted.
  2. Each claim sits in a tier, and every high-tier item has a primary source you opened.
  3. Every number carries its population and its year, not just its digits.
  4. Every quotation exists verbatim in the original, attributed to the right speaker.
  5. Causal claims have evidence of causation, or the wording says association.
  6. The links resolve, and the sources say what you say they say.

A closing thought on proportion: the goal is not zero risk, it is knowing where the risk sits. A piece whose load-bearing claims have all been checked can carry some lighter material around it. A piece whose central statistic arrived from a chat window cannot, however clean the rest of it reads. The same discipline applies to anything you compress before publishing, which is why the long-document summarising method and this routine share the same insistence on locations, and why our AI research workflow puts verification at the end rather than in the middle.

Frequently asked questions

How long does fact-checking an AI draft take?

Far less than writing the draft from scratch. Extracting the claims takes a few minutes, and verification is quick once you separate high-risk items from low-risk ones. In practice a short article needs a focused pass rather than a full investigation, provided you check the load-bearing claims against primary sources before you touch the rest.

What is the most common error in AI output?

Confident specificity. A figure with a decimal point, a dated rule or a named study reads as verified even when it was invented, because precision signals accuracy to a reader. The habit that catches most of these is simple: if a claim looks too precise to be casual, treat it as unchecked until you have opened the source yourself.

Should I fact-check opinions as well as facts?

Not in the same way. Opinions do not need verification, but they do need attribution — make clear whose view it is. Facts, figures, dates, names, quotations and legal claims require sources. Predictions and framing choices should be labelled as such, so a reader can tell where your evidence ends and your judgement begins.
